name: Vera Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive an old Fiat Panda round the valley, which used to be all coal mines and is now mostly older people whose kids moved away. I'm with a small agency, and I mostly get the dementia clients because I'm patient with them. A normal day is six or seven visits, starting at eight with Mrs Pryce, who's ninety-one and still does the crossword with me. I record my notes as voice memos and an AI app tidies them up, which saves me twenty minutes a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the dementia work, honestly, finding the one song or photo that brings someone back for a minute. What wears me out is that I'm still pretty new and I make mistakes, like forgetting a cream or mixing up which day is the bath day. And money. I'm paying off the car on finance, and if it breaks down I can't work, because there's no bus up to half the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, because the small stuff already helps me. I'd post my voice-memo trick in the carers' group, because if that's all AI ever does, everyone should at least get that bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I'm stuck in the same money trap. Low pay, a car loan, and the valley only has two agencies, so I can't shop around. AI being hype doesn't fix the fact that the bosses won't pay for our mileage properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the notes app and look at other small tools, like the one that reminds me which client has which cream. I'd start the access course at the college in Merthyr Road, the one you need before nursing. And I'd get my girlfriend Aisha to help me make a budget, because she's better with money than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. If AI stays this small, I'll still be a carer talking care notes into my phone in a lay-by, and still paid less than my petrol costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if the car breaks down you can't work. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twice last winter. The second time it was the clutch, three hundred pounds, and I had to borrow it from Aisha. I lost two days of visits, and the agency gave my clients to someone else for the week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day already. What would you actually miss if it stayed this small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hope, really. I'd been thinking AI might change how care works, maybe make room for better jobs. If it all stays the same, the valley stays the same too.

say: I'd say it's a **shame**, because the small stuff already helps me.
I'd share my **voice-memo trick** in the carers' group.
think: I'm still stuck in the same **money trap** with a car loan.
The valley has only **two agencies**, so I can't shop around.
do: Keep using the **notes app** and try a cream-reminder tool.
Start the **access course** at the college, the step before nursing.
Make a **budget** with Aisha, who's better with money.
feel: **Restless**, wanting more than the same money trap.
S0.quote: If AI stays this small, I'll still be a carer talking care notes into my phone in a lay-by, and still paid less than my petrol costs.
fieldNote: Vera's job hangs on an **old car**; a clutch repair cost her two days' work.
She is already the **early adopter**, saving twenty minutes a day with AI.
She blames bosses for unpaid **mileage**, not technology.

steps.text: Start the access course at the college before nursing
Try a reminder app for each client's creams
Make a monthly budget with Aisha's help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bring it on, and show the agency how it can help. I'd be telling the union that we need to make sure the time saved goes to clients and not to profit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's probably good for me. I'm already the one who knows the apps, so I could be the one who trains others. My hands-on work wouldn't change for years, and the paperwork side would get easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager, Bethan, to make me the agency's tech champion, the person who shows everyone the new tools, for an extra fifty pence an hour. I'd keep doing the access course at night. I'd push in the union for any time saved to go back into longer visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly, with a little knot in my stomach for the others. I'm the carer who already talks to an app in a lay-by, so AI taking over the office paperwork is the first change that might actually pay me more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the agency's office look like in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller, probably. The rota and the invoicing would be done by software, and they'd keep one coordinator instead of three. That's sad for them, but it might mean the agency survives against the big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the carers who don't take to the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that worries me. Some of the older carers, like Lynne, who's been doing this twenty years, would hate it. I'd want to help them, not show them up.

I'd tell the union the **time saved** must go to clients, not profit.
think: It's probably **good for me**, since I already know the apps.
My **hands-on work** wouldn't change for years.

Keep doing the **access course** at night.
Push the union for **longer visits** with any time saved.
feel: **Excited**, with a small knot for colleagues like Lynne.
S1.quote: I'm the carer who already talks to an app in a lay-by, so AI taking over the office paperwork is the first change that might actually pay me more.
fieldNote: Vera sees Steady Disruption as a **chance** to earn more, not a threat.
She worries about **older carers** like Lynne being shown up.
Her progressive streak shows: savings should go to **clients**, not profit.

steps.text: Ask Bethan for the tech champion role and fifty pence more

Push the union to turn saved time into longer visits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment the government has to step in, with something like a basic income for everyone. I'd say it loudly, online and at the union, because the money from robots has to be shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it scares me. Thinking AI in 2028 would wipe out the nursing jobs I'm training for, at least the paperwork side. Then robots in 2031 would take the hands-on care, which is all I've got. I'd be thirty, with a car loan and no degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch from the nursing course to something about robots, like learning to set up and fix care robots. I'd pay the car off as fast as I could and stop buying anything we don't need. I'd join a campaign for a basic income, because I think that's the only real fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I'm running for a train I might miss. Two years until thinking AI and five until robots means I'd be retraining in a hurry with a car loan and no degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're quick with new tech. Does that help when the robots come in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, maybe. Someone has to set the robots up in people's homes and calm the families down. But I don't know if three years is enough for someone like me to learn it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Aisha about money, the week this was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we stop all the extras, the takeaways and the gym. We'd sit down with her budget sheet on a Sunday and look at whether we could move somewhere with more jobs. I'd hate leaving the valley, but I might have to.

say: I'd say the government must step in with a **basic income** for everyone.
I'd argue the money from robots has to be **shared**.
think: Thinking AI in 2028 would wipe out the **nursing jobs** I'm training for.
Robots in 2031 would leave me at thirty with a **car loan** and no degree.
do: Switch from nursing to **setting up care robots** in people's homes.
Pay off the **car** fast and stop every extra spend.
feel: Like running for a **train** she might miss.
S2.quote: Two years until thinking AI and five until robots means I'd be retraining in a hurry with a car loan and no degree.
fieldNote: Vera's adaptability **pivots** instantly from nursing to robot set-up work.
She'd consider **leaving the valley** with Aisha, though she'd hate it.
Her politics move straight to a **basic income**.

steps.text: Swap the nursing access course for care-robot installation training
Pay off the Fiat finance early and drop takeaways
Join a campaign for a basic income
Look at moving out of the valley with Aisha

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that the money from robots has to be shared. But I'd also say five years is enough to train carers properly if anyone bothers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one I could probably handle. I'd finish the access course, and maybe get into something where I work with the robots, setting them up and checking on clients. I'd be about thirty-five when the robots come, which isn't too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the access course in the first year, then look for training in care technology, maybe through the agency or the college. I'd use every AI tool going at work to stay ahead. I'd try to clear the car loan and save a little, maybe fifty pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it's the good kind, like before an exam. With five years, I could be the one who sets up the care robots in the valley instead of the one they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years before thinking AI, eight before robots. How does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the gap between panicking and planning. With two years I'd grab any course. With five I'd pick the right one and actually finish it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the valley would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lynne and the others who've done this twenty years. And the clients, honestly. Mrs Pryce would hate a robot doing her crossword with her, and I'd hate it for her.

say: I'd say the money from robots has to be **shared**.
I'd say five years is enough to **train carers** properly.
think: This one I could probably **handle** with the right course.
I'd be about **thirty-five** when the robots come, which isn't too late.

S3.quote: With five years, I could be the one who sets up the care robots in the valley instead of the one they replace.
fieldNote: Five years turns Vera's panic into **planning**.
She still worries most about **Lynne** and Mrs Pryce, not herself.
She'd aim to be the one who **sets up** robots rather than is replaced.

steps.text: Finish the access course within the first year
Use every AI tool the agency offers to stay ahead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do this properly, so there's no excuse. I'd want the union to write the rules for robots in care, before the companies do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be all right. Ten years is enough to get qualified as a nursing associate, then learn the robot side as well. I'd be forty when they come, with a proper trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the access course, then do the nursing associate training while working part time. I'd keep using AI tools every day and learn the care robots as soon as there were any to learn on. I'd try to save a little each month, maybe with Aisha.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost hopeful, honestly. Ten years is enough time for a girl who left school at sixteen to become a nurse who runs the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time at your age. Would you still be in care?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but not as a basic carer. I'd want to be the one who plans the care and checks the robots are doing it right. That's still care, just a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2040, in your best guess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a small team of carers and robots in the valley, I hope. Maybe still visiting Mrs Pryce's daughter by then. I don't know, but I'd like to be the one who decides how it's done.

I'd want the union to **write the rules** for robots in care.
think: I'd be **all right**, qualified as a nursing associate by then.
I'd be **forty** when robots come, with a proper trade.

fieldNote: With ten years, Vera sees a route to **nursing** plus robot oversight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough time to retrain properly on a carer's wage. What would help is free training for carers, paid while we study, and a basic income so nobody's scared to change. Nobody in the valley is scared of robots. People here are scared of being poor again, like when the mines shut.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many of us want to stay in care even if robots come. I don't want a different job. I want a better version of this one.

headlineQuote: Nobody in the valley is scared of robots. People here are scared of being poor again, like when the mines shut.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old** carer in a former mining valley, driving an old Fiat on finance.
She takes the **dementia clients** and uses AI every day for her care notes.
She lives with her girlfriend **Aisha** and is studying toward nursing.
She moves from **alarmed** under fast AGI to almost hopeful with ten years' warning.
Her answer is **training**, a basic income, and staying in care in a new role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to retrain on a carer's wage.
whatWouldHelp: Free **paid training** for carers while they study.
A **basic income** so nobody is scared to change.
